full_prose_under_review.title: Prescriptions from Out-of-State Practitioners
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: Three pathways, their windows, and the duties each places on the pharmacist
learning_objectives: Identify which of the three out-of-state pathways the facts fall into before reaching for any number.
Apply the correct filling window: 30 days for schedules III through VI, 5 days for either schedule II route.
Apply the authenticity duty to every pathway and the telephone-verification duty to the pathways that carry it.
Separate the window that authorizes the fill from the five-day limit on an initial partial dispensing.
Carry out the post-fill reporting duty the schedule II pathways impose.
State what the later paragraphs of s. 18(d1/2) permit a Massachusetts retail pharmacy to do, and on what conditions.

orientation.text: Massachusetts does not have one out-of-state rule; it has three, and they sit in adjacent subsections of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18. Subsection (c) covers schedules III through VI, issued by an authorized practitioner who is duly licensed and authorized to engage in prescriptive practice, duly registered in the state wherein he resides, if required, and duly registered under federal law to write prescriptions. Subsection (d) covers a NONNARCOTIC schedule II prescription, issued by a practitioner licensed and authorized to engage in prescriptive practice and registered in another state where the practitioner resides or practices, if required, and registered under federal law. Subsection (d1/2), except as provided in s. 18A, covers a NARCOTIC schedule II prescription and narrows the issuing states to Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth. Read those conditions as the statute writes them: (c) speaks of the state wherein the practitioner resides, (d) and (d1/2) of the state where the practitioner resides or practices, and all three require federal registration to write prescriptions. These subsections matter because the prescriber is not registered under chapter 94C; a practitioner who is authorized to prescribe controlled substances and registered under the chapter issues under s. 18(a), and these windows do not govern that prescription. The first question on any out-of-state fact pattern is which of the three you are in, because the window and the duties both change -- and s. 18(d1/2) does not end with its first paragraph.

The windows are the easy half, provided they are read as the statute states them. Each paragraph authorizes a FILLING rather than a presentation: s. 18(c) is valid only for the purpose of authorizing the filling of prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days, and s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) apply only to authorizations for the filling, within the commonwealth, of prescriptions issued within the preceding five days. The operative date is therefore the date of the fill: a prescription handed across the counter inside the window but filled after it has closed is not one the paragraph authorizes, and the same five-day limit governs a full fill and an initial partial fill alike. Count the days the way the Board directs, taking the day after the prescription was written as day one, under 247 CMR 9.04(10). And do not reach past the Massachusetts window for a federal one: the federal six-month schedule III and IV period does not license a fill that no Massachusetts paragraph authorizes.

The duties are where candidates go wrong. Every one of the three subsections places a duty on the FILLING PHARMACIST to determine, in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment, that the prescription is authentic and valid. On top of that, subsection (c) adds telephone or other verification only where the substance is in schedules III to V, while subsections (d) and (d1/2) each state the verification duty independently for their schedule II routes. The practical shape is counter-intuitive: verification is NOT a schedule III to V speciality, and schedule VI is the single pathway that carries the authenticity duty without it. On each of these pathways a pharmacist shall not fill a prescription for which verification cannot be obtained, and shall not be held liable for refusing to fill one, provided documented good faith efforts were made to determine its authenticity and validity.

Two duties survive the fill itself. If the prescription is a schedule II filled under (d) or (d1/2), the pharmacist must deliver a copy to the Department within 30 days of the FILLING, and the copy must not include the patient's name and address; neither the copy nor the information on it is a public record. And if such a prescription is partially dispensed, s. 18(d3/4) requires the initial partial dispensing to be filled not more than five days after the prescription issue date, while the remaining portion must be filled not later than 30 days after that date and only by the same pharmacy that dispensed the lesser quantity. Two different five-day figures therefore live in this area, and they are not the same rule. One is the window within which the out-of-state subsection authorizes filling the prescription at all; the other is the limit on the initial partial dispensing of a prescription filled pursuant to those subsections, and only it brings the 30-day remainder clock with it. The regulation that implements the partial-fill limit, 105 CMR 721.055(A), states it as a presentation deadline and triggers it off the face of the prescription: where the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth, the prescription must be presented for initial partial fill not later than five calendar days after the issue date.

Subsection (d1/2) continues past the paragraph most candidates learn, and the continuation is substantive. A first further paragraph provides that nothing in the subsection prohibits a retail pharmacy operating within the commonwealth from filling narcotic schedule II prescriptions for residents of states other than Maine and the states contiguous with the commonwealth, on six stated conditions: the pharmacy is licensed for retail here and, if applicable, registered with the appropriate regulatory authorities in the state from which the prescription is received and with the Drug Enforcement Administration; the prescription is filled by a pharmacist licensed and registered in the state it originates from, where that state requires it, and is written by a practitioner -- or by a nurse practitioner or physician assistant the origin state authorizes -- licensed and registered in the same state as, or a state contiguous to, the state of delivery and registered under federal law; it reaches the pharmacy by mail, commercial carrier or an equivalent electronic means federal law authorizes; the pharmacist determines that it is authentic, valid, legitimate and legal in the state it came from and verifies it, and any delivery complies in full with that state's laws and regulations on the issuance and filling of prescriptions; the pharmacy complies with the delivery state's reporting requirements, including enrolment in and adherence to its prescription monitoring program where applicable; and the substances go by mail or commercial carrier to a verified address in the patient's state of residence, entering no hands in the commonwealth outside the postal service or the carrier chosen. A second further paragraph provides that nothing in the subsection prohibits the same retail pharmacy from filling narcotic schedule II prescriptions for patients admitted to a long-term care facility in Maine or a contiguous state, provided the pharmacy holds that licensure and registration and the medications are delivered directly to the facility by a courier the pharmacy employs or contracts. Neither paragraph makes the pharmacy a mail order pharmacy, which the section states nothing in it authorizes; each describes a Massachusetts retail pharmacy filling and shipping on conditions the paragraph itself sets.

worked_examples.scenario: A New Hampshire physician's written prescription for amphetamine salts, a nonnarcotic Schedule II substance, is presented at your Massachusetts pharmacy three days after it was issued. The prescriber is registered in New Hampshire and under federal law. Your technician says verification is only needed for Schedules III through V. What do you do?
steps: Identify the pathway. A nonnarcotic Schedule II from an out-of-state practitioner is M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d), not s. 18(c) and not the narcotic route in s. 18(d1/2).

Check the issuing conditions the subsection states: licensed and authorized to engage in prescriptive practice, registered in another state where the practitioner resides or practices if that state requires it, and registered under federal law to write prescriptions. The facts give you both registrations.

Check the window against the fill rather than the counter. s. 18(d) authorizes the filling of prescriptions issued within the preceding five days; at three days, counting the day after it was written as day one, a fill today is inside it.

Apply the duty the pathway states. s. 18(d) requires the filling pharmacist both to determine authenticity and validity in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment and to verify the prescription by telephone or other means. The technician is wrong: verification is not a Schedule III through V speciality.
If verification cannot be obtained, do not fill. Document the good faith efforts; the statute protects a pharmacist who refuses on that basis.
After filling, start the post-fill clock: a copy goes to the Department within 30 days of the filling, without the patient's name and address.
worked_examples.resolution: Verify before filling. Skipping verification here would fill a Schedule II prescription without a step s. 18(d) makes a precondition of the fill, and the Department copy is still owed 30 days after the filling.

worked_examples.scenario: A Connecticut nurse practitioner's prescription for a Schedule VI antihypertensive is presented 20 days after issue. Your colleague wants to telephone the prescriber's office to verify before filling, and is frustrated that nobody is answering after hours. Must the fill wait for that call?
steps: Identify the pathway. Schedule VI from an out-of-state practitioner falls under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which reaches schedules III to VI inclusive and asks that the practitioner be duly licensed and authorized to engage in prescriptive practice, duly registered in the state wherein the practitioner resides if that state requires it, and duly registered under federal law.
Check the window. s. 18(c) authorizes filling a prescription issued within the preceding 30 days; at 20 days, counting the day after it was written as day one, a fill today is inside it.

Read the duty precisely. s. 18(c) imposes the authenticity-and-validity determination on every prescription it reaches, but conditions telephone or other verification on the substance being in schedules III to V. Schedule VI is outside that condition.

So the pharmacist still has to be satisfied, in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment, that the prescription is authentic and valid -- but the separate telephone-verification duty is not triggered.
worked_examples.resolution: No. The fill does not wait on a verification call that this pathway does not require. Schedule VI is the one out-of-state pathway carrying the authenticity duty without the telephone-verification duty, and this is the distinction the wording of s. 18(c) turns on.

worked_examples.scenario: A Rhode Island physician's oxycodone prescription, a Schedule II narcotic, is presented four days after issue. The patient asks for only part of the quantity today. Which five-day rule are you applying, and what closes when?
steps: Identify the pathway. A narcotic Schedule II from a contiguous state is s. 18(d1/2), and Rhode Island is contiguous with the commonwealth.

The first five-day rule is the filling window: s. 18(d1/2) applies only to authorizations for the filling of prescriptions issued within the preceding five days, so it governs whether anything may be dispensed on this prescription today. At four days it does.
Verify the prescription by telephone or other means, and do not fill if verification cannot be obtained.

The second five-day rule is the partial-fill limit, and it is a different rule with a different source. s. 18(d3/4) requires the initial partial dispensing of a prescription filled pursuant to s. 18(d) or (d1/2) to be filled not more than five days after the issue date, and 105 CMR 721.055(A) states the same limit as a presentation deadline of five calendar days where the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth. Both point at today's dispensing; what the partial-fill rule adds is what happens next.
Follow the remainder to its own clock: it may be filled not later than 30 days after the issue date, and only by this pharmacy, which is the clock that outlives the five-day window.
worked_examples.resolution: Both five-day rules are satisfied today, and they are not the same rule: one decides whether the out-of-state subsection authorizes a fill at all, the other governs the initial partial dispensing and carries the 30-day remainder clock. Note the partial dispensing and the quantity in the patient record, keep any remainder at this pharmacy, complete it within 30 days of the issue date, and send the anonymised Department copy within 30 days of the filling.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy receives by commercial carrier a written prescription for a narcotic Schedule II substance, written by a practitioner licensed and registered in Pennsylvania and registered under federal law, for a patient who lives in Pennsylvania, to be shipped to the patient's home there. A colleague says Massachusetts allows narcotic Schedule II fills only on prescriptions from Maine or a contiguous state, so this one must be refused.
steps: Identify where in s. 18(d1/2) these facts sit. The subsection's first paragraph is about who may issue a narcotic Schedule II prescription for filling here; a later paragraph of the same subsection provides that nothing in it prohibits a retail pharmacy operating within the commonwealth from filling such prescriptions for residents of states other than Maine and the contiguous states.

Work through that paragraph's conditions instead of assuming them. The pharmacy must be licensed for retail by the commonwealth and, if applicable, registered with the appropriate regulatory authorities in the state from which the prescription is received and with the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the prescription must be filled by a pharmacist licensed and registered in the originating state where that state requires it.

Check the prescriber against the state of delivery rather than against Massachusetts. The writer must be licensed and authorized to engage in prescriptive practice and registered in the same state as, or a state contiguous to, the state to which the prescription is to be delivered, and registered under federal law; an authorized nurse practitioner or physician assistant qualifies on the same terms.

Check how the prescription arrived and how the drug will leave. It must be received by mail, commercial carrier or an equivalent electronic means authorized by federal law, and the substance must be delivered by mail or commercial carrier to a verified address in the patient's state of residence, without entering the hands of anyone in the commonwealth outside the postal service or the carrier selected.

Apply the duties the paragraph attaches to the fill itself: determine that the prescription is authentic, valid, legitimate and legal in the state it came from, verify it by telephonic or other means, do not fill it if verification cannot be obtained, comply in full with that state's laws and regulations on the issuance and filling of prescriptions, and meet its reporting requirements, including enrolment in and adherence to its prescription monitoring program where that applies.
worked_examples.resolution: The colleague has read the first paragraph of s. 18(d1/2) and stopped. A Massachusetts retail pharmacy may fill this prescription and ship it, provided every condition the later paragraph states is met, and the reason to refuse would be a failed verification or an unmet condition rather than the prescriber's state. The conditions to work are the ones that paragraph states, including the delivery state's own law on the issuance and filling of prescriptions; and the paragraph does not turn the pharmacy into a mail order pharmacy, which the section says nothing in it authorizes.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which out-of-state pathway carries the authenticity duty but NOT the telephone-verification duty, and why?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Schedule VI under s. 18(c). The subsection reaches schedules III to VI but conditions verification on the substance being in schedules III to V.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Out-of-state filling windows: schedules III through VI, ______ days; either schedule II route, ______ days. What date must fall inside the window?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 30; 5. Each subsection authorizes the FILLING of prescriptions issued within the preceding window, so the fill must happen while the prescription is still that young; a prescription presented in time but filled later is outside the authorization.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: verification by telephone or other means is required only for out-of-state schedule III through V prescriptions.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) each state the verification duty independently for the nonnarcotic and narcotic schedule II routes.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under the first paragraph of s. 18(d1/2), where must the practitioner be registered, and what do the later paragraphs of that subsection add?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Maine, or a state contiguous with the commonwealth. Two later paragraphs provide that nothing in the subsection prohibits a retail pharmacy operating here from filling narcotic schedule II prescriptions for residents of other states, delivered by mail or commercial carrier to a verified address in the patient's state of residence, or for patients admitted to a long-term care facility in Maine or a contiguous state, delivered directly to the facility by a courier the pharmacy employs or contracts -- each on the conditions its own paragraph states.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name three conditions the s. 18(d1/2) paragraph attaches to filling a narcotic schedule II prescription for a resident of another state.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Any three of: Massachusetts retail licensure plus registration with the origin state's regulatory authorities and the Drug Enforcement Administration as applicable; a filling pharmacist licensed and registered in the originating state where it requires that; a prescriber licensed and registered in the same state as, or a state contiguous to, the state of delivery and registered under federal law; receipt by mail, commercial carrier or an equivalent federally authorized electronic means; a determination that the prescription is authentic, valid, legitimate and legal in the state it came from, with verification; compliance with the delivery state's prescription laws and reporting requirements, including its monitoring program; and delivery by mail or commercial carrier to a verified address in the patient's state of residence.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A pharmacist refuses an out-of-state prescription because verification could not be obtained. What protects them, and what is the condition?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The statute provides they shall not be held liable for the refusal, provided documented good faith efforts were made to determine authenticity and validity.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The Department copy after filling an out-of-state Schedule II prescription is due within ______, measured from ______, and must omit ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: 30 days; the filling; the patient's name and address.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the two distinct five-day rules in this area, and say what each one decides.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The filling window in s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2), which decides whether the subsection authorizes filling the prescription here at all; and the initial partial-dispensing limit in s. 18(d3/4), implemented by 105 CMR 721.055(A), which governs the initial partial dispensing of a prescription filled under those subsections and carries the 30-day remainder clock with it.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: In deciding whether a prescription is within date, which day is day one, and how does 105 CMR 721.055(A) count?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 9.04(10): the day after the prescription was written is day one, so the issue date itself is not counted. 105 CMR 721.055(A) runs five CALENDAR days from the prescription issue date, and attaches that limit where the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does s. 18(c) require of the issuing practitioner, in its own words, and how does that differ from s. 18(d)?
retrieval_prompts.answer: That the practitioner be duly licensed and authorized to engage in prescriptive practice, duly registered in the state wherein he resides, if required, and duly registered under federal law to write prescriptions. Section 18(d) instead speaks of registration in another state where the practitioner resides or practices, if required, and likewise requires federal registration.

quick_review.text: An authorized out-of-state practitioner's schedule III through VI prescription is fillable in Massachusetts under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which authorizes filling only prescriptions issued within the preceding 30 days.
Either out-of-state schedule II route authorizes filling only a prescription issued within the preceding five days, under separate subsections with their own issuing conditions.

All three subsections require the issuing practitioner to be registered under federal law to write prescriptions; s. 18(c) asks for registration in the state wherein the practitioner resides, if required, while s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) ask for the state where the practitioner resides or practices.
The first paragraph of the schedule II narcotic route reaches a practitioner registered in Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth.

Later paragraphs of s. 18(d1/2) let a retail pharmacy operating here fill narcotic schedule II prescriptions for residents of other states, delivered by mail or commercial carrier to a verified address in the patient's state of residence, and for patients admitted to a long-term care facility in Maine or a contiguous state, delivered by the pharmacy's own courier, each on its stated conditions.

Every out-of-state pathway requires the filling pharmacist to determine authenticity and validity; telephone verification is additionally required on schedules III through V and on both schedule II routes, leaving schedule VI as the one pathway without it.

Where the out-of-state prescription is oral and in schedules III through V, the pharmacist records having requested that the practitioner deliver or mail a written prescription to the dispensing pharmacy within seven days or the shorter period federal law requires.

A prescription filled under s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2) has its own five-day limit on the INITIAL PARTIAL DISPENSING, separate from the window that authorizes the fill, and the remaining portion runs to 30 days after the issue date at the same pharmacy.

105 CMR 721.055(A) states the initial partial-fill limit as five calendar days from the prescription issue date and triggers it off the prescriber's address on the prescription being outside the Commonwealth.
In determining whether a prescription is within date, 247 CMR 9.04(10) counts the day after the prescription was written as day one.
After filling an out-of-state schedule II prescription the pharmacist delivers a copy to the Department within 30 days, with the patient's name and address removed.

decision_logic.condition: An out-of-state practitioner's prescription is presented.
decision_logic.action: Identify the subsection first: schedules III through VI run on s. 18(c) and 30 days, a nonnarcotic schedule II on s. 18(d) and five days, a narcotic schedule II on s. 18(d1/2), five days and a narrower list of issuing states. Check the issuing condition that subsection states, federal registration included.

decision_logic.condition: You have identified the pathway and are deciding whether the window is open.
decision_logic.action: Measure to the fill, not to the presentation: the subsection authorizes filling a prescription issued within the preceding 30 or five days, counting the day after the prescription was written as day one.

decision_logic.condition: The prescription is inside the window of its pathway.
decision_logic.action: Determine, in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment, that the prescription is authentic and valid. Then verify by telephone or other means unless the substance is schedule VI, and do not fill if verification cannot be obtained.
Refuse the fill and document the good faith efforts made; the statute protects the refusal on that basis.

decision_logic.condition: The out-of-state schedule III-V prescription was communicated orally.
decision_logic.action: Record that you requested the practitioner deliver or mail the written prescription to the dispensing pharmacy within seven days or the shorter period federal law requires; the period runs on the practitioner's delivery.

decision_logic.condition: An out-of-state schedule II prescription under s. 18(d) or (d1/2) is partially dispensed.
decision_logic.action: Fill the initial partial dispensing not more than five days after the issue date, treating 105 CMR 721.055(A) as five calendar days from that date where the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth; note the partial fill and quantity in the patient record; keep any remainder at this pharmacy and fill it not later than 30 days after the issue date.

decision_logic.condition: A narcotic schedule II prescription is to be filled here for a resident of another state, or for a patient in a long-term care facility in Maine or a contiguous state.
decision_logic.action: Work the conditions of the applicable later paragraph of s. 18(d1/2): Massachusetts retail licensure and the registrations it names; for the other-state paragraph, a prescriber registered in the same state as, or a state contiguous to, the state of delivery, receipt by mail, carrier or an equivalent federally authorized electronic means, authenticity, validity, legitimacy and legality in the originating state with verification, compliance with the delivery state's prescription and reporting law, and delivery by mail or carrier to a verified address in the patient's state of residence; for the long-term care paragraph, delivery directly to the facility by the pharmacy's employed or contracted courier.

decision_logic.condition: You have filled an out-of-state schedule II prescription.
decision_logic.action: Deliver a copy to the Department within 30 days of the filling, excluding the patient's name and address.

ma_vs_federal.text: The federal six-month schedule III and IV clock does not license an out-of-state prescription that no Massachusetts paragraph authorizes filling; the Massachusetts window is the gate that closes first.
The out-of-state oral schedule III through V follow-up period is stated as seven days or the shorter period federal law requires, so a shorter federal period governs where one exists.

The s. 18(d1/2) paragraph for residents of other states does not displace the delivery state's law: it conditions the fill on full compliance with that state's laws and regulations on the issuance and filling of prescriptions and on its reporting requirements, including its prescription monitoring program where applicable.

exceptions.text: The five-day schedule II window sits in separate subsections that also carry their own conditions on which issuing states qualify, so it is not simply a shorter version of the same rule.

These subsections matter where the prescriber is not registered under chapter 94C: a practitioner who is authorized to prescribe controlled substances and registered under the chapter issues under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(a), and the five-day filling window in s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) does not govern that prescription.

Later paragraphs of s. 18(d1/2) provide that nothing in the subsection prohibits a retail pharmacy operating within the commonwealth from filling narcotic schedule II prescriptions for residents of states other than Maine and the contiguous states, on six stated conditions ending in mail or commercial-carrier delivery to a verified address in the patient's state of residence, or for patients admitted to a long-term care facility in Maine or a contiguous state, delivered directly to the facility by a courier the pharmacy employs or contracts.
Schedule VI is the one out-of-state pathway carrying the authenticity duty without the separate telephone-verification duty.

The out-of-state schedule II subsections authorize the filling only. They do not authorize the practitioner to possess, administer or dispense controlled substances as provided in section 9 or to practise within the commonwealth, and the section states that nothing in it authorizes a mail order pharmacy -- which is the backdrop to the later paragraphs of s. 18(d1/2), where it is a Massachusetts retail pharmacy that fills and ships.

timing_deadlines.event: Filling an out-of-state schedule III through VI prescription under s. 18(c)
timing_deadlines.timeframe: The prescription must have been issued within the preceding 30 days
timing_deadlines.consequence: Outside the window this pathway does not authorize the fill at all.

timing_deadlines.event: Filling an out-of-state schedule II prescription under s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2)
timing_deadlines.timeframe: The prescription must have been issued within the preceding 5 days
timing_deadlines.consequence: The 30-day figure does not carry across to schedule II, and the limit reaches a full fill as well as an initial partial fill.

timing_deadlines.event: Initial partial dispensing of a schedule II prescription filled pursuant to s. 18(d) or (d1/2)
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 5 days after the prescription issue date
timing_deadlines.consequence: 105 CMR 721.055(A) states the same limit as presentation for initial partial fill within five calendar days, where the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth.

timing_deadlines.event: Remaining portion of that partially dispensed prescription
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not later than 30 days after the prescription issue date
timing_deadlines.consequence: The remainder closes on the issue-date clock and only at the same pharmacy that dispensed the lesser quantity.

timing_deadlines.event: Practitioner delivery of an out-of-state oral schedule III-V written follow-up
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Within 7 days or the shorter period federal law requires
timing_deadlines.consequence: The period governs the practitioner's delivery; what the pharmacist owes is the record that the request was made.

timing_deadlines.event: Department copy after filling an out-of-state schedule II prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: This clock runs from the filling, unlike the filling windows and the partial-fill limits in this section, which run from the prescription issue date.

forms_records.text: On the out-of-state oral schedule III-V pathway the pharmacist records having requested the practitioner's written prescription.

An initial partial dispensing and any later dispensing of the remaining portion carry the s. 18(d3/4) patient-record notation of the partial fill and the quantity dispensed, accessible to the prescriber on request; 105 CMR 721.055(C) states the same duty for the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee.
The Department copy excludes the patient's name and address, and neither the copy nor its contents is a public record.
Where verification cannot be obtained, the good faith efforts made are themselves the record that protects the refusal.

A pharmacy filling under the s. 18(d1/2) paragraph for residents of other states must comply with the delivery state's reporting requirements, including enrolment in and adherence to that state's prescription monitoring program or an equivalent program, where applicable.

role_duties.duty: Determine authenticity and validity on every out-of-state pathway, and verify by telephone or other means on every pathway except schedule VI.
Refuse to fill an out-of-state prescription for which verification cannot be obtained.
Measure each window to the fill, counting the day after the prescription was written as day one.
Deliver the anonymised Department copy within 30 days of filling an out-of-state schedule II prescription.

common_traps.text: Treating verification as a schedule III through V feature fills an out-of-state nonnarcotic schedule II prescription without a step s. 18(d) makes a precondition of the fill.
Carrying the 30-day out-of-state window to a schedule II prescription accepts one that Massachusetts authorizes filling only within five days of issue.

Reading the window as a deadline for presenting the prescription lets a pharmacist accept it in time and fill it out of time; the subsections authorize the filling of prescriptions issued within the preceding window.
Filling an out-of-state schedule III-V prescription on the federal six-month clock skips both the Massachusetts window and the verification gate.

Treating the seven-day follow-up period as the pharmacist's deadline reverses the timed event: the period runs on the practitioner's delivery of the written prescription, and the pharmacist's duty is to record the request.

Reading the five-day figure as one rule merges the window that authorizes the fill with the separate limit on an initial partial dispensing, and loses the 30-day remainder clock that only the second carries.
Counting the initial partial-fill limit in business days, or from something other than the prescription issue date, misses that 105 CMR 721.055(A) counts five calendar days from that date.
Measuring the Department copy's 30 days from the issue date rather than from the filling misses that this is the one duty here keyed to the dispensing event.
Demanding a verification call on a schedule VI out-of-state prescription applies a duty s. 18(c) conditions on schedules III to V.

Refusing a narcotic schedule II prescription for a resident of another state because the prescriber is outside Maine and the contiguous states stops at the first paragraph of s. 18(d1/2) and misses the later paragraph that permits the fill on stated conditions.

authority.name: Out-of-state Schedule III through VI prescriptions

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: An authorized out-of-state practitioner may issue a Schedule III through VI prescription filled in Massachusetts within 30 days of issue; Schedule III through V prescriptions require pharmacist verification.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) a prescription for a controlled substance contained in SCHEDULES III TO VI, INCLUSIVE, as defined in section 3, may also be issued by an authorized practitioner who is DULY LICENSED AND AUTHORIZED TO ENGAGE IN PRESCRIPTIVE PRACTICE and DULY REGISTERED IN THE STATE WHEREIN HE RESIDES, IF REQUIRED, and DULY REGISTERED UNDER FEDERAL LAW TO WRITE PRESCRIPTIONS. That wording differs from s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2), which speak of registration in another state where the practitioner RESIDES OR PRACTICES, if required. The paragraph is VALID ONLY FOR THE PURPOSE OF AUTHORIZING THE FILLING OF PRESCRIPTIONS, ISSUED WITHIN THE PRECEDING THIRTY DAYS, and shall not authorize the practitioner to process, administer or dispense controlled substances as provided in section 9 or to practice within the commonwealth. A prescription issued under the paragraph SHALL BE ISSUED IN THE MANNER PRESCRIBED IN SECTION 22, and all relevant provisions of chapter 94C apply to the practitioner and the prescription. Nothing contained in section 18 shall be deemed to authorize any mail order pharmacies.
exceptions: The state-registration condition applies 'if required', so a practitioner whose state of residence does not require registration meets it without one; the federal-registration condition carries no such qualifier.
A practitioner authorized to prescribe controlled substances and registered under chapter 94C issues under s. 18(a), and s. 18(c) is not the authority for that prescription.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(a) a prescription for a controlled substance may be issued only by a practitioner who is authorized to prescribe controlled substances and registered pursuant to chapter 94C. Section 18(d) provides that a prescription for a nonnarcotic substance in Schedule II may also be issued by a practitioner who is licensed and authorized to engage in prescriptive practice and registered in another state where the practitioner resides or practices, if required, and registered under federal law to write prescriptions. Section 18(d1/2), except as provided in s. 18A, provides the same for a narcotic substance in Schedule II where the practitioner is so licensed and registered in Maine or in a state contiguous with the commonwealth. Each subsection is only for the purpose of authorizing the filling, within the commonwealth, of prescriptions issued within the preceding five days, and does not authorize the practitioner to possess, administer or dispense controlled substances under s. 9 or to practice within the commonwealth. A Schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner who is not registered under chapter 94C is therefore fillable in Massachusetts only under s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2), and only if it was issued within the preceding five days, whether the fill is full or partial.
exceptions: A practitioner who is authorized to prescribe controlled substances and registered under chapter 94C issues under s. 18(a), and the five-day filling window of s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) does not govern that prescription.
The narcotic route in s. 18(d1/2) reaches only practitioners registered in Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth, and is subject to s. 18A.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Massachusetts may fill a Schedule II narcotic prescription from Maine or a contiguous state within five days of issue after required authentication and verification; separate delivery provisions govern certain out-of-state residents.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws
authority.section: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d1/2), unnumbered paragraphs following the main paragraph

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d1/2) continues after its main paragraph with two further paragraphs. The first provides that NOTHING IN THE SUBSECTION SHALL BE INTERPRETED TO PROHIBIT A RETAIL PHARMACY OPERATING WITHIN THE COMMONWEALTH FROM FILLING PRESCRIPTIONS FOR A NARCOTIC SUBSTANCE CONTAINED IN SCHEDULE II TO RESIDENTS OF STATES OTHER THAN MAINE AND THE STATES CONTIGUOUS WITH THE COMMONWEALTH, PROVIDED THAT: (1) the pharmacy shall be licensed for retail by the commonwealth and, if applicable, registered with the appropriate regulatory authorities in the state from which the prescription is received and the United States Drug Enforcement Administration, as applicable, for the dispensing of controlled substances; (2) the prescription shall be filled by a pharmacist licensed and registered in the state from which the prescription originates, if that state requires such registration and licensing, and shall be written by a practitioner licensed and authorized to engage in prescriptive practice and registered in the same state or a contiguous state to where the prescription is to be delivered and registered under federal law to write prescriptions, or shall be written by a nurse practitioner or physician assistant authorized by the state of the prescription's origin to write it, licensed and registered in the same state or a contiguous state to where the prescription is to be delivered and registered under federal law to write prescriptions; (3) the prescription shall be RECEIVED by the retail pharmacy VIA MAIL OR COMMERCIAL CARRIER or through an equivalent electronic means as may be authorized by federal law; (4) the registered pharmacist filling it shall determine, in accordance with professional standards and personal judgment, that it is AUTHENTIC, VALID, LEGITIMATE AND LEGAL IN THE STATE FROM WHICH IT IS RECEIVED and SHALL VERIFY the prescription by telephonic or other means, a pharmacist shall not fill a prescription for which verification cannot be obtained, and any delivery of controlled substances to residents of another state shall be in FULL COMPLIANCE WITH ALL LAWS AND REGULATIONS OF THAT STATE relative to the issuance and filling of prescriptions; (5) the pharmacy shall comply with ALL REPORTING REQUIREMENTS OF THE STATE TO WHICH THE PRESCRIPTION IS DELIVERED, including but not limited to enrollment in and adherence to the rules, regulations and requirements of that state's prescription monitoring program or an equivalent program, where applicable; and (6) any substances delivered shall be DELIVERED VIA MAIL OR BY A COMMERCIAL CARRIER TO A VERIFIED ADDRESS IN THE STATE OF RESIDENCE of the person for whom the prescription was written and shall not enter into the hands of any person in the commonwealth not directly associated by employment or subcontract with the United States Postal Service or commercial carrier selected for the purpose. The second paragraph provides that NOTHING IN THE SUBSECTION SHALL PROHIBIT A RETAIL PHARMACY OPERATING WITHIN THE COMMONWEALTH FROM FILLING PRESCRIPTIONS FOR A NARCOTIC SUBSTANCE CONTAINED IN SCHEDULE II FOR PATIENTS ADMITTED TO A LONG-TERM CARE FACILITY IN MAINE OR A STATE CONTIGUOUS WITH THE COMMONWEALTH, PROVIDED THAT (i) the pharmacy is licensed for retail by the commonwealth and, if applicable, registered with the appropriate regulatory authorities in the state from which the prescription is received and the United States Drug Enforcement Administration, as applicable, for the dispensing of controlled substances; and (ii) the medications are DELIVERED DIRECTLY TO THE LONG-TERM CARE FACILITY BY A COURIER EMPLOYED OR CONTRACTED BY THE RETAIL PHARMACY. The main paragraph of the same subsection states that nothing in the section shall authorize a mail-order pharmacy.
exceptions: Each paragraph speaks of a retail pharmacy operating within the commonwealth and licensed for retail by the commonwealth; the main paragraph of the subsection states that nothing in the section shall authorize a mail-order pharmacy.

Delivery under the first paragraph is by mail or commercial carrier to a verified address in the patient's state of residence; under the second, directly to the long-term care facility by a courier employed or contracted by the retail pharmacy.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: All three out-of-state pathways place a duty on the FILLING PHARMACIST, and they are not identical. Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) it is the duty of the pharmacist filling a schedule III through VI out-of-state prescription TO DETERMINE, IN ACCORDANCE WITH PROFESSIONAL STANDARDS AND PERSONAL JUDGMENT, THAT THE PRESCRIPTION IS AUTHENTIC AND VALID; and, PROVIDED THE SUBSTANCE IS IN SCHEDULES III TO V INCLUSIVE, the pharmacist SHALL ALSO VERIFY THE PRESCRIPTION BY TELEPHONE OR OTHER MEANS. A schedule VI out-of-state prescription therefore carries the authenticity duty WITHOUT the separate telephone-verification duty. Under s. 18(d) a pharmacist filling an out-of-state NONNARCOTIC schedule II prescription SHALL determine authenticity and validity AND SHALL VERIFY the prescription by telephone or other means; s. 18(d1/2) imposes the same on the NARCOTIC schedule II route. On every one of these pathways A PHARMACIST SHALL NOT FILL A PRESCRIPTION FOR WHICH VERIFICATION CANNOT BE OBTAINED, and A PHARMACIST SHALL NOT BE HELD LIABLE FOR REFUSING to fill such a prescription PROVIDED DOCUMENTED GOOD FAITH EFFORTS were made to determine its authenticity and validity.
exceptions: Schedule VI is the one out-of-state pathway carrying the authenticity duty without the telephone-verification duty, because s. 18(c) conditions verification on the substance being in schedules III to V.
The liability protection for refusing depends on documented good faith efforts, not on the refusal alone.

authority.name: Massachusetts oral Schedule III through V follow-up request

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: For an oral Schedule III through V prescription issued under the out-of-state pathway, the pharmacist records requesting a written prescription within seven days or the shorter federal period.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws
authority.section: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4), read with s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2)

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) a pharmacist filling a Schedule II prescription SHALL, if requested by the patient, dispense a lesser quantity; ONLY THE SAME PHARMACY that dispensed the lesser quantity may dispense the remaining portion; a notation of the partial fill and quantity goes in the patient record, accessible to the prescriber on request; and the remaining portion MUST BE FILLED NOT LATER THAN 30 DAYS AFTER THE PRESCRIPTION ISSUE DATE. The separate FIVE-DAY limit on the INITIAL partial dispensing applies only to a prescription FILLED PURSUANT TO SUBSECTION (d) OR (d1/2) -- respectively a nonnarcotic Schedule II prescription issued by an out-of-state practitioner, and a narcotic Schedule II prescription issued by a practitioner registered in Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth.

105 CMR 721.055(A) states the Massachusetts patient-requested partial fill as a duty: a pharmacist filling a Prescription for a schedule II controlled substance SHALL, IF REQUESTED BY THE PATIENT, dispense the substance in a lesser quantity than indicated, pursuant to M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4). It then supplies the operative trigger for the five-day limit: IF THE PRESCRIPTION WAS ISSUED BY A PRESCRIBER FROM A LOCATION OTHER THAN THE COMMONWEALTH, AS INDICATED BY THE ADDRESS OF THE PRESCRIBER ON THE PRESCRIPTION, the Prescription MUST BE PRESENTED FOR INITIAL PARTIAL FILL NOT LATER THAN FIVE CALENDAR DAYS after the Prescription issue date. That is a different test from the statute's 'filled pursuant to subsection (d) or (d1/2)': the pharmacist reads the address on the face of the prescription rather than adjudicating which statutory subsection the prescription travelled under, and the count is expressly in CALENDAR days. Under 721.055(B) the remaining portion may be filled on patient request provided only the same pharmacy that dispensed the lesser quantity dispenses it and it is filled not later than 30 days after the issue date, and under 721.055(C) the pharmacist or designee makes a notation in the patient record, accessible to the prescribing practitioner on request, of the partial fill and the quantity dispensed.
exceptions: The five-calendar-day limit attaches only where the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth.

authority.name: Out-of-state nonnarcotic Schedule II prescriptions, Department copy

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Where a Schedule II prescription is filled under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d) (a nonnarcotic Schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner) or s. 18(d1/2) (a narcotic Schedule II prescription from a practitioner registered in Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth), the pharmacist SHALL, WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER FILLING the prescription, DELIVER TO THE DEPARTMENT A COPY OF EACH SUCH SCHEDULE II PRESCRIPTION. The copy SHALL NOT INCLUDE THE NAME AND ADDRESS OF THE PATIENT for whom the prescription was issued, and neither the copy nor the information on it is a public record within M.G.L. c. 4, s. 7; both are subject to the restrictions in M.G.L. c. 66A, s. 2. Both subsections state this duty in the same terms. Neither subsection authorizes the out-of-state practitioner to possess, administer or dispense controlled substances under s. 9 or to practise within the commonwealth, and neither authorizes mail order pharmacies.
exceptions: The copy is anonymised: the patient's name and address are excluded.
The copy is not a public record and is subject to the M.G.L. c. 66A, s. 2 restrictions.

authority.name: Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: In order to determine whether a prescription is WITHIN DATE, a pharmacist shall count the DAY AFTER the prescription was written as DAY ONE. The issue date itself is not counted, so a period measured in days runs from the following day.

full_prose_under_review.title: Massachusetts Schedule VI
learning_objectives: Recognize Schedule VI as the Massachusetts controlled-substance schedule for prescription drugs outside Schedules I through V, rather than as a federal controlled schedule.
Apply Massachusetts prescription elements, oral documentation, electronic-prescribing exceptions, and transfer rules without inventing federal consequences.
Apply the Schedule VI validity clock and the additional-drug consequences instead of treating Schedule VI as a consequence-free label.
Recognise that the Schedule VI classification carries its own scope-of-practice consequence for who may transfer a prescription.
Identify every date gate that can bar a Schedule VI prescription, including the out-of-state 30-day window that sits alongside the one-year validity clock.

orientation.text: Massachusetts Schedule VI is the residual schedule: it holds prescription drugs that Massachusetts has not otherwise placed in Schedules I through V. It is a controlled-substance schedule all the same. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 defines a controlled substance as a drug, substance, controlled substance analogue or immediate precursor in any schedule or class referred to in that chapter, and s. 2(a) establishes the sixth schedule alongside the five that incorporate the federal schedules, so the ordinary prescription drug that carries no federal schedule is, in Massachusetts, a Schedule VI controlled substance. Two consequences follow, and they pull in opposite directions. Schedule VI has no federal counterpart -- 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (E) define Massachusetts Schedules I through V as the drugs listed in 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15, and 700.002(F) leaves Schedule VI the prescription drugs outside them -- so Schedule VI status does not by itself make a drug federally controlled, and federal controlled-substance mechanics do not automatically travel with the label. Because Schedule VI is nonetheless a Massachusetts controlled-substance schedule, a Massachusetts rule that speaks to controlled substances reaches Schedule VI unless that rule carves Schedule VI out: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(f), for instance, allows no refill of a controlled-substance prescription unless the original provides for refilling and specifies the number of refills. Reading the label as a synonym for unregulated is the single most productive source of wrong answers in this area.

Every rule taught in this section is Massachusetts law, and it does not all come from one regulator. M.G.L. c. 94C is the statute above both. The Department of Public Health writes 105 CMR 700.000 and 105 CMR 721.000, and from there come the classification itself, the prescription-format scheme, the electronic-prescribing exceptions and the prescription monitoring program. The Board of Registration in Pharmacy writes 247 CMR, and from there come the Schedule VI validity clock, the within-date counting convention and the transfer framework. Some duties are stated twice over. A customer identifier must be presented under the Board's 247 CMR 9.04(14) and, for a pharmacy subject to the monitoring-program reporting requirement, under the Department's 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3); M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c)(2) directs the Department to require each pharmacy to collect and report a customer identification number for each monitored prescription. Even inside the Board's own chapter a Schedule VI question can turn on two different one-year rules that sit in two different sections of 247 CMR 9.00 and answer two different questions: 247 CMR 9.04(12) says how long the prescription stays valid, and 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) says how long it stays transferable. Neither restates the other, and a candidate who has collapsed them into one rule will misread whichever question is actually being asked.

On format, Massachusetts starts from a default that every prescription generated in the Commonwealth must be electronic, and then lists the prescriptions excepted from it. The default is statutory and it names Schedule VI: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 17(c) provides that a controlled substance included in Schedule III, IV, V or VI shall not be dispensed without an electronic prescription from a practitioner, and s. 23(g) directs prescribers to issue an electronic prescription for all controlled substances and medical devices. The exception is therefore not a gap the statute left. Section 23(h) directs the commissioner, through regulation, to establish exceptions to s. 17 and s. 23(g) authorizing the limited use of a written and oral prescription where appropriate, and limits them to an enumerated list; Schedule VI is one of the enumerated exceptions the commissioner made, at 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9), which is why a Schedule VI prescription may lawfully arrive written or oral. Knowing where the exception comes from matters because it tells you what could move it: the mandate is in the statute, the exception is in a regulation made under s. 23(h), and the six subjects clauses (i) through (vi) name -- veterinarians, temporary technological or electrical failure, a time-limited hardship waiver, emergency situations, prescriptions that cannot be issued electronically under federal or state law, and prescriptions issued outside the jurisdiction of the commonwealth -- do not include Schedule VI, leaving it to the residual clause (vii), under which the commissioner must file a written justification with the house and senate committees on ways and means, the joint committee on public health and the joint committee on mental health, substance use and recovery 90 days before promulgating or amending such a regulation. The exception is narrow in exactly the way candidates tend to forget: it lifts the electronic-format mandate and nothing else. A written Schedule VI prescription must still carry the practitioner's signature and be either transmitted by facsimile or similar technology or written on a tamper-resistant form, and a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and shall not be filled. An oral Schedule VI prescription must still be reduced to writing immediately with the information the statute requires. Among the oral-prescription duties, the one Schedule VI escapes is the practitioner's later follow-up prescription: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) says in its own terms that its requirements do not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI, and the follow-up in 105 CMR 721.070(B) is written for oral prescriptions in Schedules II through V. The Failover device points the same way: it is defined as a document that originates as a Schedule VI electronic prescription, so no other schedule can produce one.

A Schedule VI prescription can be stopped by more than one clock, and the exam rewards knowing which clock the facts have started. The general one is the validity limit: a prescription for a Schedule VI medication is valid for one year from the date of issue, and a licensee may not refill it after one year. A second one attaches to the prescriber rather than the drug. An authorized out-of-state practitioner may issue a Schedule III through VI prescription for filling in Massachusetts, but M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) authorizes filling only prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days, and it is that paragraph, not the one-year rule, that makes the out-of-state prescription fillable here in the first place. Both clocks are counted the same way, because in determining whether a prescription is within date the pharmacist counts the day after the prescription was written as day one. The two clocks fail differently, and the fourteen-day continuation belongs to only one of them: 247 CMR 9.04(12) opens it where a Schedule VI prescription expires or has no remaining refills and the pharmacist is unable to obtain prescriber authorization in a timely manner. Nothing in it reopens the thirty-day authorization in s. 18(c), so an out-of-state prescription past that window is not a candidate for a bridge supply on the strength of the continuation.

Transfer is the other place where the Schedule VI label changes the analysis, and it does so in the pharmacy's direction as well as the patient's. Under 247 CMR 9.14 a pharmacy shall transfer a prescription to another pharmacy at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, and it may act as the patient's agent to facilitate that transfer. A pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription, so neither a standing refusal to transfer nor a transfer charge is a matter the pharmacy gets to decide for itself. Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedule III through V prescriptions, carrying up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, subject to the separate one-year transfer bar. Schedule VI is also the only schedule for which a certified pharmacy technician may perform the transfer, and then only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

Finally, the Schedule VI label is not a promise that no monitoring or identification duty will ever attach. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(a)(1) has the Department monitor all schedule II to V controlled substances and certain additional drugs, meaning substances the Department determines to carry a bona fide potential for abuse, and 105 CMR 700.001 defines an Additional Drug as a controlled substance in Schedule VI so determined. The Commissioner may make that determination for the purposes of 105 CMR 700.012, weighing factors such as a risk of addiction, known recreational use, known regular diversion for misuse, or a known contribution to overdose, and on making it notifies all dispensers that they must begin reporting the dispensing of that drug. Once a Schedule VI drug is an additional drug, dispensing it requires a customer identifier from the ultimate user or their agent, subject to the documented-hardship route, under both 247 CMR 9.04(14) and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3); the Failover route closes, because a Failover does not qualify where the prescription is for an additional drug, and the Department's manual states what the pharmacist does instead: on receiving a Failover for gabapentin, or any other medication designated as an Additional Drug, the pharmacist may not dispense the medication and must contact the prescriber for a new written or oral prescription; and the dispensing has to be reported on two clocks that apply together. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c) requires the information to be submitted at least once every 24 hours, and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) requires transmission by the end of the next business day, each transmission carrying everything dispensed since the previous one. The operative deadline is whichever of the two arrives first, and across a weekend or a holiday that is always the statute: a Friday dispensing cannot wait for the end of Monday, which the regulation read alone would allow. The label describes the starting point, not the whole of the drug's regulatory position.

Written-format requirements: signature, plus facsimile transmission or a tamper-resistant form
