comparison_tables.title: Transfer of a Schedule VI prescription: what 247 CMR 9.14 settles for the pharmacy

cells: May the pharmacy decline the request as a matter of store policy?
No. A pharmacy shall transfer a prescription to another pharmacy at the request of a patient or the patient's agent, in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy.
May the pharmacy arrange the transfer on the patient's behalf?
Yes. The pharmacy may act as the patient's agent in order to facilitate a transfer.
May the pharmacy charge for the transfer?
No. A pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription.
How many refills move with it?
Up to the maximum number of remaining refills authorized by the prescriber, Schedule VI transferring in the same manner as Schedules III through V.
Is the prescription too old to transfer?
It is once it is more than one year from the date the prescription was issued.
May a certified pharmacy technician carry it out?
Yes, for Schedule VI only, and only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient asks Pharmacy B to obtain a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription from Pharmacy A. The prescription was issued ten months ago and has three authorized refills remaining. Pharmacy A says it does not transfer prescriptions as a matter of store policy, and that if it did it would charge the patient a transfer fee first. Pharmacy B has a certified pharmacy technician available and the pharmacist on duty approves the technician's participation.
steps: Classify the drug before anything else. It is not in Massachusetts Schedules I through V, so it is a Schedule VI controlled substance under Massachusetts law, and because no federal schedule lists it the federal transfer mechanics do not reach it.

Check the age of the prescription against the transfer bar rather than the validity clock. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) bars transfer of a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills more than one year from the date it was issued; ten months is inside that limit.

Test Pharmacy A's policy against 247 CMR 9.14(1). A pharmacy shall transfer a prescription at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, so a standing refusal to transfer cannot stand against the request.
Test the fee against 247 CMR 9.14(3), which provides that a pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription. There is no discretion to price the transfer.

Settle what moves. Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedules III through V, and may be transferred up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, so all three remaining refills may travel.

Settle who may act. A certified pharmacy technician may perform a Schedule VI transfer with the approval of the pharmacist on duty, and that authority is confined to Schedule VI; do not generalise it to any other schedule.
worked_examples.resolution: The transfer proceeds promptly, without a fee, carrying the three remaining refills, and the certified technician may carry it out with the pharmacist's approval. The error the scenario invites is treating a no-transfer policy and a transfer charge as pharmacy discretion, when 247 CMR 9.14(1) and 9.14(3) remove both; a second error is reaching for a six-month cutoff in place of the one-year transfer limit.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient presents a Schedule VI prescription written forty-five days ago by a practitioner licensed and registered in New Hampshire, whose address on the prescription is a New Hampshire office. The patient points out that Massachusetts Schedule VI prescriptions are good for a year, so the prescription must still be fillable.
steps: Confirm the patient is right about the clock they have named. Under 247 CMR 9.04(12) the prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue, and forty-five days is well inside that.

Then ask the question the patient has not asked: what makes an out-of-state practitioner's prescription fillable in Massachusetts at all. That authorization is M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which reaches prescriptions in Schedules III to VI inclusive.

Read the limit that paragraph attaches to its own grant. It is valid only for the purpose of authorizing the filling of prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days, so it is a second date gate rather than a restatement of the first.
Count the days the way the Board directs, taking the day after the prescription was written as day one. Forty-five days still falls outside the thirty-day window however the count is started.

Do not look for a verification step that will rescue it. The express duty to verify the prescription by telephone or other means runs to Schedules III through V; for a Schedule VI prescription the pharmacist's duty is the general one to determine that the prescription is authentic and valid, and neither duty extends the thirty-day window.

Do not reach for the fourteen-day continuation either. 247 CMR 9.04(12) opens it where a Schedule VI prescription expires or has no remaining refills and authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner; this prescription has not expired, and in any event nothing in the continuation reopens the thirty-day authorization in s. 18(c).
worked_examples.resolution: The prescription may not be filled on the out-of-state authorization, because the paragraph that authorizes filling it here reaches only prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days. The error the scenario invites is answering from the one-year Schedule VI validity clock alone and never asking where the prescriber wrote from.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient arrives on a Saturday evening out of a maintenance medication. The Schedule VI prescription on file was issued fourteen months ago and shows refills that were never used. A colleague says the prescription has plainly expired, so the fourteen-day continuation is simply what you dispense in that situation.
steps: Establish that the prescription itself is spent. It was valid for one year from the date of issue, and a licensee may not refill a Schedule VI prescription after one year, so unused refills on a fourteen-month-old prescription do not survive the expiry.

Read the continuation as the conditional allowance it is. It opens where a Schedule VI prescription expires or has no remaining refills AND the pharmacist is unable to obtain prescriber authorization in a timely manner; the inability condition governs the expiry branch exactly as it governs the no-refills-remaining branch.

Attempt the authorization first. Try the prescriber, or whoever is covering, and record the attempt. Only once authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner does the professional-judgment allowance become available at all.

If it does open, respect the ceiling. The pharmacist in his or her professional judgment may dispense a quantity not to exceed fourteen days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging. It is a bridge, not a refill, and it does not renew the expired prescription.

Check the setting before applying any of this. 247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 247 CMR 9.04(12), so the validity clock and the continuation attached to it do not reach that facility type.
worked_examples.resolution: Attempt the prescriber before dispensing anything; the fourteen-day continuation becomes available only after that attempt fails to produce timely authorization. The error the colleague makes is reading the expiry branch as self-executing, which drops the inability-to-obtain-authorization condition the regulation attaches to both branches.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Massachusetts Schedule VI carries two separate one-year rules. State each one and what it measures.
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 9.04(12): a Schedule VI prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue and may not be refilled after one year. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c): a pharmacy may not transfer a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills more than one year from the date the prescription was issued. One measures fillability, the other transferability.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A pharmacy tells a patient it does not transfer prescriptions, and that in any event it charges for a transfer. Which two provisions dispose of that?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 9.14(1) requires the pharmacy to transfer at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, and 247 CMR 9.14(3) provides that a pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Besides the one-year validity clock, what second date gate can stop a Schedule VI prescription, and where does it come from?
retrieval_prompts.answer: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c): an authorized out-of-state practitioner's prescription in Schedules III to VI inclusive may be filled in Massachusetts only if it was issued within the preceding thirty days.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which oral-prescription duty does Schedule VI escape, and which does it keep?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It escapes the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) follow-up prescription, which states that its requirements do not apply to Schedule VI. It keeps the duty to reduce the oral prescription to writing immediately with the information the statute requires.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception sits at 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9). What does it not excuse?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It lifts the electronic-format mandate only. The statutory prescription elements still apply, a written prescription must still carry the practitioner's signature and be transmitted by facsimile or written on a tamper-resistant form, and a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and shall not be filled.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Massachusetts excepts Schedule VI from electronic prescribing at 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9). What does the statute itself say about Schedule VI and electronic prescriptions, and how do the two fit together?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The statute imposes the mandate and names Schedule VI. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 17(c) provides that a controlled substance included in Schedule III, IV, V or VI shall not be dispensed without an electronic prescription from a practitioner, and s. 23(g) directs prescribers to issue an electronic prescription for all controlled substances and medical devices. Section 23(h) then directs the commissioner, through regulation, to establish exceptions to s. 17 and s. 23(g) authorizing the limited use of a written and oral prescription where appropriate, and limits them to an enumerated list. Schedule VI is not among the six subjects clauses (i) through (vi) name, so it rests on clause (vii), other exceptions as the commissioner determines necessary, which the commissioner may promulgate or amend only after filing a written justification with the house and senate committees on ways and means, the joint committee on public health and the joint committee on mental health, substance use and recovery 90 days beforehand. The Schedule VI exception is a regulatory choice made under a statutory grant, which is why it is found in 105 CMR 721.070(A) and not in the statute.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What turns an ordinary Schedule VI drug into one carrying monitoring and identification duties?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The Commissioner's determination under 105 CMR 700.012(C)(8) that it is an additional drug carrying a bona fide potential for abuse. On that determination dispensers are notified that they must begin reporting it, and a customer identifier is required at dispensing under 247 CMR 9.04(14) and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3), subject to the documented-hardship route. The reporting then runs on two clocks: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c) requires submission at least once every 24 hours, and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) requires transmission by the end of the next business day, covering everything dispensed since the previous transmission.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A document that began as a Schedule VI electronic prescription failed in transmission and arrived as a computer-generated facsimile. What is it, and what does it not owe?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A Failover. It is considered an oral prescription and requires no written or electronic follow-up prescription, provided the three conditions in 105 CMR 721.020(G) hold and the prescription is not for an additional drug.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: In deciding whether a prescription is within date, which day is day one?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The day after the prescription was written; the issue date itself is not counted.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name two things 105 CMR 721.020 requires on the face of a prescription that the element list in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(a) does not.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The quantity of dosage units, under 105 CMR 721.020(D)(3), alongside the name, dosage and strength per dosage unit that the statute requires; and the name of the supervising qualified healthcare professional on a prescription issued by a certified nurse practitioner, psychiatric nurse mental health clinical specialist or certified registered nurse anesthetist who is not authorized for independent practice, under 721.020(E). The refill statement in 721.020(D)(6) is not one of the additions, because s. 22(a) requires it too.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Schedule VI additional drug is dispensed on a Friday afternoon. When must the dispensing reach the Department?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Whichever limit arrives first, because both apply: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c) requires the information to be submitted at least once every 24 hours, and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) requires transmission by the end of the next business day, carrying everything dispensed since the previous transmission. Across the weekend the statute is the stricter, so waiting for the end of Monday is not an option.

quick_review.text: Massachusetts Schedule VI includes prescription drugs not otherwise placed in Massachusetts Schedules I through V.

Every Schedule VI drug is a controlled substance under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 and s. 2(a), while 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (E) make Massachusetts Schedules I through V the federal lists, so Schedule VI is a Massachusetts controlled-substance schedule with no federal counterpart; a Massachusetts rule written for controlled substances, such as the refill condition in s. 23(f), reaches it unless the rule carves Schedule VI out.
Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing requirement, while all other validity requirements remain applicable.
An oral controlled-substance prescription must be reduced to writing immediately with the required information; the separate duty to deliver a later follow-up prescription does not reach Schedule VI.
A Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue, and a licensee may not refill it after one year.

A Schedule VI drug the Department designates as an additional drug becomes reportable to the prescription monitoring program by a pharmacy subject to 105 CMR 700.012, and its dispensing requires a customer identifier, subject to the documented-hardship route.

A pharmacy shall transfer a prescription to another pharmacy at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, and may act as the patient's agent to facilitate the transfer; a standing policy of refusing transfers cannot displace that duty.
A pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription.
Schedule VI is the only schedule for which a certified pharmacy technician may perform a prescription transfer, and then only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

A Schedule VI prescription may be transferred up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized under 247 CMR 9.14(4)(b); the federal one-time transfer limit in 21 CFR 1306.25(a) reaches prescriptions for substances listed in federal Schedules III, IV and V, so it does not reach a Schedule VI drug that no federal schedule lists.

A prescription written by an authorized out-of-state practitioner is fillable in Massachusetts under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which reaches Schedules III to VI inclusive and authorizes filling only prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days; that is a second date gate on a Schedule VI prescription, distinct from the one-year validity clock.

Prescription monitoring data for a reportable dispensing runs on two limits that apply together: at least once every 24 hours under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c), and by the end of the next business day under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5), each transmission covering everything dispensed since the previous one.

decision_logic.condition: A prescription drug is not in Massachusetts Schedules I-V.
decision_logic.action: Classify it under Schedule VI, then identify the separate rule governing validity, documentation, dispensing, or transfer.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule VI prescription is written or oral rather than electronic.
decision_logic.action: Do not reject it solely for that format; apply the Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception and all remaining prescription requirements, including the form requirements that still govern a written prescription.

decision_logic.condition: A patient requests transfer of a Schedule VI prescription with authorized refills remaining.
decision_logic.action: Act on the request rather than declining it: 247 CMR 9.14(1) requires the pharmacy to transfer at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, 9.14(2) lets the pharmacy act as the patient's agent to facilitate it, and 9.14(3) forbids charging a fee for the transfer. Then apply the Schedule VI mechanics under 247 CMR 9.14(4): the prescription transfers in the same manner as a Schedule III through V prescription and may carry up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, that regulation bars the transfer more than one year after issue, and a certified pharmacy technician may carry it out with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule VI prescription has expired, being presented more than one year after its issue date, or has no refills remaining, and in either case the pharmacist is unable to obtain prescriber authorization in a timely manner.
decision_logic.action: Do not refill it. The inability to obtain timely prescriber authorization conditions both branches equally, so attempt the prescriber first in the expired case exactly as in the no-refills-remaining case. Only once that attempt has failed may the pharmacist, in professional judgment, dispense a quantity not to exceed 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging.

decision_logic.condition: The Schedule VI medication being dispensed has been designated an additional drug by the Department.
decision_logic.action: Obtain a customer identifier under 247 CMR 9.04(14) and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3), using the documented hardship route only on its own terms, and treat the dispensing as reportable, submitting at least once every 24 hours under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c) and by the end of the next business day under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5).

decision_logic.condition: The Schedule VI prescription was written by a practitioner licensed and registered outside Massachusetts.
decision_logic.action: Apply the out-of-state date gate before the validity clock: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) authorizes filling such a prescription only if it was issued within the preceding thirty days, counting the day after it was written as day one. Determine that the prescription is authentic and valid; note that the express telephone-or-other-means verification requirement runs to Schedules III through V rather than to Schedule VI.

decision_logic.condition: A document that began as a Schedule VI electronic prescription arrives as a computer-generated facsimile, and the drug on it has been designated an additional drug.
decision_logic.action: Do not dispense on the facsimile, and do not treat the failed condition as something a later prescription can cure. The Department's Electronic Prescribing and Dispensing Manual states that on receiving a Failover for gabapentin, or any other medication designated as an Additional Drug, the pharmacist may not dispense the medication and must instead contact the prescriber for a new written or oral prescription. The additional-drug condition is the fourth of the conditions a Failover must satisfy, and failing it takes the document outside the Failover route altogether rather than converting it into an oral prescription that owes a follow-up; a Failover that does qualify is dispensed as an oral prescription and needs no additional written follow-up.

ma_vs_federal.text: Schedule VI is a Massachusetts controlled-substance classification: it makes the drug a controlled substance under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 and s. 2(a), and it does not itself make the drug federally controlled, because Massachusetts Schedules I through V are the federal lists that Schedule VI sits outside.
A Schedule VI drug the Department designates as an additional drug carries Massachusetts prescription-monitoring and customer-identifier duties that the Schedule VI label alone does not imply.

The Massachusetts route for an out-of-state practitioner's prescription is M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which reaches Schedules III to VI inclusive; because Schedule VI has no federal counterpart, that thirty-day window is a purely Massachusetts limit and has no federal analogue to be read against it.

exceptions.text: The Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception removes that format mandate, not the required prescription elements or oral documentation duties.

Where a Schedule VI prescription has expired or has no remaining refills and prescriber authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner, the pharmacist may in professional judgment dispense a quantity not exceeding 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging.

247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 247 CMR 9.04(12), and from 9.04(10) and 9.04(14) as well, so the Board's Schedule VI validity clock, its day-counting convention and its customer-identifier requirement do not reach that facility type. The exclusion reaches only those Board paragraphs: for a pharmacy subject to 105 CMR 700.012, the Department's own customer-identifier requirement in 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3) continues to apply.
In deciding whether a prescription is within date the pharmacist counts the day after it was written as day one, so the Schedule VI one-year period does not include the issue date itself.

The follow-up duty Schedule VI escapes is the practitioner's obligation under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) to deliver an electronic prescription within 2 days, or a written one within not more than 7 days, or the shorter period federal law requires, where the prescriber holds an electronic-prescribing exception under s. 23(h); the parallel follow-up in 105 CMR 721.070(B) is written for oral prescriptions in Schedules II through V and does not reach Schedule VI either.

The Failover is a Schedule VI device: a document that began as a Schedule VI electronic prescription, failed in transmission and arrived as a computer-generated facsimile counts as an oral prescription needing no follow-up, provided its three conditions hold and the drug is not an additional drug.

105 CMR 700.012 does not apply to dispensing pursuant to a medication order to an inpatient in a hospital, so neither the monitoring-program reporting duty nor the Department's customer-identifier requirement reaches that dispensing, whatever the drug; 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) otherwise reaches every pharmacy registered with the Commissioner that dispenses a Schedule II through V controlled substance or an additional drug pursuant to a prescription.

timing_deadlines.event: Remaining-refill transfer of a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 1 year after issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) does not permit that remaining-refill transfer after the regulatory one-year limit.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: 1 year from the date of issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: A licensee may not refill a Schedule VI prescription after one year.

timing_deadlines.event: Filling in Massachusetts a Schedule III through VI prescription issued by an authorized out-of-state practitioner
timing_deadlines.consequence: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) authorizes filling only prescriptions issued within that window, so an older out-of-state Schedule VI prescription is barred even though the one-year validity period has not run.

timing_deadlines.event: Transmission of prescription monitoring data for a reportable dispensing, under the Department's regulation
timing_deadlines.timeframe: By the end of the next business day
timing_deadlines.consequence: 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) also requires each transmission to carry every controlled substance dispensed since the previous one.

timing_deadlines.event: Submission of prescription monitoring information, under the statute
timing_deadlines.consequence: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c) sets this limit alongside the Department's transmission requirement, so a dispensing reported only at the end of the next business day is late whenever more than 24 hours have passed since the pharmacy's previous submission, as after a Friday dispensing held until Monday.

forms_records.text: The pharmacist must immediately reduce an oral controlled-substance prescription to writing with the required Massachusetts prescription information.

A customer identifier must be obtained when dispensing a Schedule VI additional drug, under 247 CMR 9.04(14) and, for a pharmacy subject to 105 CMR 700.012, under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3); the hardship route requires a documented reason and the recipient's printed name and address and signature, with an electronic signature in the case of an electronic prescription.

A written Schedule VI prescription must carry the practitioner's signature and must either be transmitted by facsimile or similar technology or be written on a tamper-resistant form consistent with federal Medicaid requirements; a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and may not be filled.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(a) requires a practitioner who dispenses a controlled substance by issuing a written or electronic prescription to state on it the practitioner's name, address and registration number, the date of delivery of the prescription, the name, dosage and strength per dosage unit of the controlled substance, the name and address of the patient unless it is a veterinary prescription, the directions for use and any cautionary statements required, and a statement indicating the number of times to be refilled. Read that as the list the statute itself imposes, not as a closed inventory of everything a Massachusetts prescription must carry: the Massachusetts prescription-format regulations reach the same prescription and impose their own requirements alongside the statute.

The format regulation states content the statutory element list does not, and relaxes the patient-identification element in cases the statute does not name: 105 CMR 721.020(D)(3) requires the QUANTITY OF DOSAGE UNITS alongside the name, dosage and strength per dosage unit; (D)(6) repeats the statutory statement indicating the number of times to be refilled; and under (D)(4) the patient's name and address MAY BE LEFT BLANK not only on a veterinary prescription but also on one for naloxone or another Department-approved opioid antagonist and on one issued under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7), for expedited partner therapy for the treatment of chlamydia, or (A)(12), for a declared public health emergency, for diseases dangerous to public health including sexually transmitted infections, or for any other urgent public health matter.

A prescription issued by a certified nurse practitioner, psychiatric nurse mental health clinical specialist or certified registered nurse anesthetist must also carry the name of the supervising qualified healthcare professional, unless that nurse is authorized for independent practice.

role_duties.duty: Validate required prescription elements even when the Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception applies.
Check the Schedule VI validity clock and any additional-drug designation before dispensing rather than treating Schedule VI as consequence-free.
Act on a patient's or agent's transfer request in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, and transfer without charging a fee.
Perform a prescription transfer only for Schedule VI, and only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

common_traps.text: Reading the electronic-prescribing exception as an exemption from all prescription validity requirements is incorrect.
Treating Schedule VI as a federal schedule creates legal consequences that the Massachusetts classification does not supply.

The one-year rule in 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) governs transfer of a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills and is separate from the one-year prescription validity limit in 247 CMR 9.04(12); neither should be restated as the other.
Concluding that Schedule VI never triggers identification or monitoring-program duties overlooks Schedule VI drugs designated as additional drugs.
Generalising the certified-technician transfer authority beyond Schedule VI ignores the word only in the regulation.
Reading the electronic-prescribing exception as removing every format requirement leaves the pharmacist filling a written prescription that no permitted format supports.

Treating a refusal to transfer, or a charge for transferring, as a matter of pharmacy discretion overlooks the affirmative timely-transfer duty in 247 CMR 9.14(1) and the fee prohibition in 247 CMR 9.14(3).

Treating the one-year validity clock as the only date gate on a Schedule VI prescription misses the separate thirty-day limit M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) places on an out-of-state practitioner's Schedule III through VI prescription.

Reciting the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(a) elements as the complete set of content and exception rules for a Massachusetts prescription treats a statutory list as exhaustive, when the prescription-format regulations govern the same prescription in their own right.

Naming the veterinary prescription as the only case where the patient's name and address may be left blank misses the naloxone and opioid-antagonist limb and the two ePrescribing-exception limbs in 105 CMR 721.020(D)(4).

Reading Schedule VI as a label outside controlled-substance law misses M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 and s. 2(a), which make a Schedule VI drug a Massachusetts controlled substance, and with it every Massachusetts controlled-substance rule that does not carve Schedule VI out.

Teaching the monitoring deadline as the end of the next business day alone drops the statutory limit in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c), which requires submission at least once every 24 hours and is the stricter of the two across a weekend or holiday.

Reading the 247 CMR 9.04(15) exclusion as ending the customer-identifier duty for an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy overlooks the Department's separate requirement in 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3).

Reading 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9) as proof that the electronic-prescribing mandate never reached Schedule VI inverts the scheme: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 17(c) names Schedule VI in the mandate itself, and the exception exists because s. 23(h) directs the commissioner to establish exceptions by regulation.

Dispensing a Failover for an additional drug and waiting for a follow-up prescription gets the consequence backwards twice over: the pharmacist may not dispense that Failover at all and must contact the prescriber for a new written or oral prescription, while a Failover that does qualify is dispensed and owes no follow-up.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Massachusetts Schedule VI includes prescription drugs not otherwise placed in Schedules I through V; Schedule VI status does not itself make a drug federally controlled or routinely MassPAT-reportable.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 9.04(12) a prescription for a Schedule VI medication is valid for ONE YEAR from the date of issue and a licensee may not refill a Schedule VI prescription after one year. If a Schedule VI prescription expires or has no remaining refills and the pharmacist is unable to obtain prescriber authorization in a timely manner, the pharmacist in his or her professional judgment may dispense a quantity NOT TO EXCEED 14 DAYS or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging. Under 247 CMR 9.04(15) the requirements of 247 CMR 9.04(12) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.
exceptions: 247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 247 CMR 9.04(12).
The continuation supply is a professional-judgment allowance conditioned on inability to obtain timely prescriber authorization; it is not an automatic refill.

DCP Electronic Prescribing and Dispensing Manual

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Massachusetts generally requires covered prescriptions to be issued electronically subject to 105 CMR 721.070 exceptions and waivers. Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the state electronic-prescribing requirement under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9). Under 105 CMR 721.070(C), a pharmacist who receives an otherwise valid written or oral prescription is not required to verify that the prescription properly falls within an electronic-prescribing exception or waiver; all other prescription and controlled-substance requirements still apply.
exceptions: Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing requirement under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9).
Other enumerated exceptions and waivers may permit a covered prescription to be issued in written or oral form.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: On receiving an oral prescription for a controlled substance, the pharmacist must immediately reduce it to writing with the information required by M.G.L. c. 94C §20 and make a reasonable effort to authenticate an unfamiliar prescriber; the subsection requiring later electronic or written documentation expressly does not apply to Schedule VI.
exceptions: The follow-up prescription requirement in §20(c) does not apply to Schedule VI, but immediate reduction to writing and validity duties still apply.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A controlled-substance prescription must include the practitioner, patient, drug, strength, directions, date, registration, cautionary, and refill information required by Massachusetts law.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

authority.name: Certified pharmacy technician Schedule VI transfer scope

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under current 247 CMR 9.14, a pharmacy must timely transfer a prescription at the request of the patient or authorized agent, may act as the patient's agent to obtain the transfer, and may not charge a transfer fee. Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedule III-V prescriptions; remaining authorized refills may be transferred, but a Schedule VI prescription may not be transferred more than one year after issuance. Under 247 CMR 8.04, a certified pharmacy technician may perform a Schedule VI transfer with approval of the pharmacist on duty.
exceptions: Schedule-specific federal requirements may add restrictions for federally controlled prescriptions; do not automatically import those mechanics into a Massachusetts Schedule VI transfer.

authority.name: Massachusetts Department of Public Health regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: The Commissioner MAY DETERMINE that a drug is an 'additional drug' for the purposes of 105 CMR 700.012 because it carries a BONA FIDE POTENTIAL FOR ABUSE, based on factors including a risk of addiction alone or with a Schedule II through IV drug, known recreational use, known regular diversion for misuse, or a known contribution to overdose or regular presence in the bloodstream of persons who have overdosed. UPON MAKING SUCH A DETERMINATION THE COMMISSIONER SHALL NOTIFY ALL DISPENSERS THAT THEY MUST BEGIN TO REPORT the dispensing of that additional drug pursuant to prescription as directed in 105 CMR 700.012(A).

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: A licensee shall require a CUSTOMER IDENTIFIER, being the identification number on a valid government issued identification obtained by inspecting the identification of the ultimate user or their agent, on dispensing a controlled substance in Schedules II through V or an additional drug under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1). A licensee may dispense WITHOUT one only if it has reason to believe that refusing would cause SERIOUS HARDSHIP to the ultimate user or agent AND DOCUMENTS THE REASON, AND the recipient PRINTS name and address on the reverse of the prescription or in a prescription log AND SIGNS it. The Commissioner may waive or modify the requirement for refills, deliveries or other specified activities.
exceptions: Documented serious hardship with the recipient's printed name, address and signature
Commissioner waiver or modification for refills, deliveries or other specified activities

authority.name: Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy regulations

authority.name: Commissioner exceptions permitting written and oral prescriptions
Follow-up documentation for an oral prescription issued under an ePrescribing exception

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) a practitioner who prescribes a controlled substance by oral prescription shall cause an ELECTRONIC prescription to be delivered to the dispensing pharmacy WITHIN 2 DAYS; if the practitioner has received an electronic-prescribing exception from the commissioner under s. 23(h), the practitioner shall instead cause a WRITTEN prescription to be delivered within not more than 7 DAYS, or the shorter period required by federal law, postmarked within that period. The follow-up prescription must indicate that it documents an oral prescription, and the pharmacy attaches it to the oral prescription it reduced to writing. Under 105 CMR 721.070(B) a practitioner issuing an oral prescription for a controlled substance in SCHEDULES II THROUGH V under a 105 CMR 721.070(A) ePrescribing exception shall cause a written or electronic prescription to be delivered within not more than SEVEN BUSINESS DAYS, or the shorter period required by federal law. The s. 20(c) requirements do not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI.
exceptions: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) does not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI, although the immediate reduction to writing and the remaining validity duties still apply.
A shorter federal period controls where federal law requires one, such as the 7-day emergency oral Schedule II follow-up under 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4).

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Where state and federal law permit a WRITTEN prescription, 105 CMR 721.020(F) requires it to be issued on a form carrying the practitioner's signature and to be EITHER transmitted via facsimile or similar technology OR written on a TAMPER-RESISTANT FORM consistent with federal requirements for Medicaid. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(i) states the same at statute level. Under 105 CMR 721.040(A) a prescription in a format that does not conform is INVALID AND SHALL NOT BE FILLED. An exception that permits a written prescription therefore removes the electronic-format mandate only; the written form requirements continue to govern the prescription the exception allows.
exceptions: The facsimile route and the tamper-resistant form route are alternatives; either satisfies 105 CMR 721.020(F)(1)-(2).

authority.name: Failover treated as an oral prescription

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: 105 CMR 721.010 defines a FAILOVER as a document that ORIGINATES AS A SCHEDULE VI ELECTRONIC PRESCRIPTION, experiences an unforeseen defect during electronic transmission as outlined in Department guidance, and IS CONVERTED TO A COMPUTER GENERATED FACSIMILE. Only such a document qualifies. Under 105 CMR 721.020(G) a Failover SHALL BE CONSIDERED AN ORAL PRESCRIPTION and SHALL NOT REQUIRE a written or electronic follow-up prescription, provided all three conditions hold: it contains everything M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) requires except the practitioner's signature and is immediately entered into a compliant electronic pharmacy system or otherwise reduced to writing by the dispensing pharmacist; if the prescribing practitioner is not known to the dispensing pharmacist, that pharmacist makes a reasonable good faith effort to determine the Failover was issued by a prescribing practitioner; and the prescription is NOT FOR AN ADDITIONAL DRUG as defined in 105 CMR 700.001. Under 105 CMR 721.040(C) an electronic prescription transmitted by other means is invalid except in the event of a Failover verified under 721.020(G). A Schedule II through V oral prescription taken during a transmission outage is NOT a Failover; it falls under the separate 105 CMR 721.070(A)(2) exception and still owes the 721.070(B) follow-up.
exceptions: A Failover is Schedule VI by definition; no Schedule II through V prescription can be one.
The three conditions in 105 CMR 721.020(G)(1)-(3) are conjunctive, and they apply only after the definitional test is met.
A Failover for an Additional Drug does not qualify, so the follow-up duty continues to apply to it.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) the information 105 CMR 700.012 requires shall be transmitted to the Department or its agent, in accordance with any procedures the Commissioner establishes, BY THE END OF THE NEXT BUSINESS DAY, and shall include data for ALL CONTROLLED SUBSTANCES DISPENSED SINCE THE PREVIOUS TRANSMISSION or report, by encrypted electronic device or electronic transmission method in a format the Commissioner approves. Under 700.012(A)(6) the Commissioner may waive that method for a pharmacy unable to submit electronically.
exceptions: The Commissioner may waive the electronic transmission method for a pharmacy unable to submit by electronic means.

authority.name: Out-of-state Schedule III through VI prescriptions

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: An authorized out-of-state practitioner may issue a Schedule III through VI prescription filled in Massachusetts within 30 days of issue; Schedule III through V prescriptions require pharmacist verification.
exceptions: Apply any narrower setting-specific, product-specific, or emergency exception before the general rule.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: 105 CMR 721.020(C) requires the practitioner's NAME AND ADDRESS to be clearly indicated on the Prescription, and a hospital or clinic Prescription to carry the name and address of the hospital or clinic. 105 CMR 721.020(D) requires the Prescription to contain: (1) the REGISTRATION NUMBER of the practitioner; (2) the DATE OF ISSUANCE; (3) the name, dosage and strength per dosage unit of the controlled substance prescribed, AND THE QUANTITY OF DOSAGE UNITS; (4) the NAME AND ADDRESS OF THE PATIENT, except in a veterinary Prescription, a Prescription for naloxone or another opioid antagonist approved by the Department, or a Prescription issued under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7) or (A)(12), in which case the name and address may be left blank, and where the person taking delivery of a naloxone or other approved opioid antagonist Prescription MAY, but is not required to, be used in place of the patient's name; (5) DIRECTIONS FOR USE, including any required cautionary statements; (6) a STATEMENT INDICATING THE NUMBER OF TIMES TO BE REFILLED; and (7) for an OPIOID substance in schedule II, a NOTATION THAT THE PATIENT MAY FILL THE PRESCRIPTION, UPON REQUEST, IN AN AMOUNT LESS THAN the recommended full quantity indicated. Under 105 CMR 721.020(E) a Prescription issued by a certified nurse practitioner, psychiatric nurse mental health clinical specialist or certified registered nurse anesthetist must also contain the NAME OF THE SUPERVISING qualified healthcare professional, unless that nurse is authorized for independent practice under 244 CMR.
exceptions: The patient name and address may be left blank on a veterinary prescription, a naloxone or other Department-approved opioid antagonist prescription, or a prescription issued under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7) or (A)(12).
The supervising-professional name is not required where the issuing nurse is authorized for independent practice under 244 CMR.

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(a)(1) the department SHALL ESTABLISH AND MAINTAIN AN ELECTRONIC SYSTEM TO MONITOR the prescribing and dispensing of ALL SCHEDULE II TO V, INCLUSIVE, CONTROLLED SUBSTANCES AND CERTAIN ADDITIONAL DRUGS by all professionals licensed to prescribe or dispense such substances; for the purposes of s. 24A, 'additional drugs' means SUBSTANCES DETERMINED BY THE DEPARTMENT TO CARRY A BONA FIDE POTENTIAL FOR ABUSE. 105 CMR 700.001 defines an Additional Drug as A CONTROLLED SUBSTANCE IN SCHEDULE VI determined by the Department to carry a bona fide potential for abuse. Under s. 24A(b) the requirements of s. 24A SHALL NOT APPLY TO THE DISPENSING OF CONTROLLED SUBSTANCES TO INPATIENTS IN A HOSPITAL. Under s. 24A(c) the department shall promulgate regulations including (1) a requirement that each pharmacy that delivers a schedule II to V, inclusive, controlled substance or a substance classified as an additional drug by the department to the ultimate user shall submit to the department, by electronic means, information regarding each prescription dispensed for a drug included under subsection (a); and (2) a requirement that each pharmacy COLLECTS AND REPORTS, for each such prescription, A CUSTOMER IDENTIFICATION NUMBER and other information associated with it, as specified by the department. Each pharmacy shall submit the information in accordance with transmission methods and frequency requirements promulgated by the department; PROVIDED, HOWEVER, THAT THE INFORMATION SHALL BE SUBMITTED AT LEAST ONCE EVERY 24 HOURS. The department may issue a waiver to a pharmacy that is unable to submit prescription information by electronic means, permitting submission by other means promulgated by the department, provided that all information required by the section is submitted in that alternative format.
exceptions: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(b): the requirements of s. 24A do not apply to the dispensing of controlled substances to inpatients in a hospital.
The department may issue a waiver to a pharmacy unable to submit prescription information by electronic means, provided all required information is submitted in the alternative format.

authority.name: Prescription Monitoring Program: pharmacy reporting requirements

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3) a pharmacy that dispenses a controlled substance subject to the requirements in 105 CMR 700.012 MUST REQUIRE THAT A CUSTOMER IDENTIFIER IS PRESENTED whenever a controlled substance in Schedules II through V, OR AN ADDITIONAL DRUG, is dispensed. The pharmacy may dispense WITHOUT REVIEWING the customer identifier only if it HAS REASON TO BELIEVE THAT THE FAILURE TO DISPENSE would result in a SERIOUS HARDSHIP for the ultimate user or the ultimate user's agent, AND DOCUMENTS THE REASON; AND the ultimate user or agent PRINTS THEIR NAME AND ADDRESS ON THE REVERSE SIDE OF THE PRESCRIPTION AND SIGNS IT, or, in the case of an electronic prescription, provides an electronic signature; AND the pharmacy provides to the Department those informational fields the Department requires. Under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(4) the Commissioner may waive or modify the requirements in 105 CMR 700.012(A) for a pharmacy to report customer information as the Commissioner specifies. The requirement sits in 105 CMR 700.012, which by 700.012(A)(1) applies to every pharmacy registered with the Commissioner that dispenses pursuant to a prescription a controlled substance in Schedules II through V or one classified by the Department as an additional drug, and by 700.012(A)(2) does not apply to dispensing pursuant to a medication order to an inpatient in a hospital. The Board of Registration in Pharmacy states a customer-identifier requirement of its own in 247 CMR 9.04(14).
exceptions: The documented serious-hardship route, which also requires the recipient's printed name and address on the reverse side of the prescription and their signature, or an electronic signature on an electronic prescription, and the informational fields the Department requires.
A waiver or modification by the Commissioner under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(4).
105 CMR 700.012(A)(2): dispensing pursuant to a medication order to an inpatient in a hospital is outside 105 CMR 700.012 altogether.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws
authority.section: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1, definition of Controlled substance

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(f), no prescription for a controlled substance shall be refilled unless the original prescription provides for such refilling and unless the number of refills has been specified in said prescription. Section 1 of chapter 94C defines a controlled substance as a drug, substance, controlled substance analogue or immediate precursor in any schedule or class referred to in the chapter, and s. 2(a) establishes, besides five schedules incorporating the federal schedules, a sixth schedule which shall include all prescription drugs not included in the first five. The refill condition in s. 23(f) therefore reaches a Schedule VI prescription as well as a prescription in Schedules III through V.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 2(a) directs the commissioner of public health to establish by regulation five schedules incorporating the five schedules of controlled substances under the federal Comprehensive Drug Abuse Prevention and Control Act of 1970 or any amendment of it, and a sixth schedule which shall include all prescription drugs not included in the first five. Under s. 2(a1/2) the commissioner may delete or reschedule substances in those schedules, except that where a substance not yet scheduled under s. 2 is designated a controlled substance under the federal act, or a scheduled substance is designated a controlled substance of greater abuse liability under it, the commissioner shall, not more than 30 days after publication of final notice in the Federal Register or after the effective date of a federal statute affecting scheduling, issue a regulation controlling the substance in a schedule corresponding to the federal schedules. 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (E) define Schedules I through V as the drugs and other substances listed in 21 CFR 1308.11, 1308.12, 1308.13, 1308.14 and 1308.15 respectively, and 105 CMR 700.002(F) defines Schedule VI as all prescription drugs which are not included in any other schedule established by the Commissioner.
exceptions: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 2(a1/2) the commissioner may delete or reschedule substances, subject to the duty to control a newly federally controlled substance in a corresponding schedule within 30 days.

authority.name: Transfer between pharmacies of prescription information for Schedules III, IV, and V controlled substances for refill purposes

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Transfer of original prescription information for a controlled substance listed in Schedule III, IV or V for the purpose of refill dispensing is permissible between pharmacies ON A ONE-TIME BASIS ONLY; pharmacies electronically sharing a real-time, online database may instead transfer up to the maximum refills permitted by law and the prescriber's authorization. The transfer must be communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists, the transferring pharmacist must void and annotate the original record, and the receiving pharmacist must record the required transfer data. The procedure is permissible only if allowable under existing State or other applicable law, and it moves the prescription without creating new refill authority or restarting the six-month issue-date clock.
exceptions: Pharmacies electronically sharing a real-time, online database may transfer up to the maximum refills permitted by law and the prescriber's authorization.
The transfer procedure is permissible only if allowable under existing State or other applicable law.

authority.name: Massachusetts Department of Public Health regulations

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: 105 CMR 700.012 SHALL NOT APPLY to the dispensing PURSUANT TO A MEDICATION ORDER of a controlled substance TO AN INPATIENT IN A HOSPITAL. The reporting duty otherwise reaches every pharmacy registered with the Commissioner that dispenses a controlled substance pursuant to a prescription in Schedules II through V, or a controlled substance classified as an additional drug, and any out-of-state pharmacy delivering such a substance to a person in Massachusetts.
exceptions: Dispensing pursuant to a medication order to an inpatient in a hospital.

authority.name: Necessity of prescription for dispensing controlled substances
Electronic prescription requirement and the commissioner's exceptions

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 17(a) no controlled substance in Schedule II may be dispensed without an electronic prescription from a practitioner, except that under s. 17(b), IN EMERGENCY SITUATIONS, AS DEFINED BY THE COMMISSIONER, a schedule II, III, IV, V or VI substance may be dispensed upon written prescription or oral prescription IN ACCORDANCE WITH SECTION 20 AND RELATED REGULATIONS; under s. 17(c) a controlled substance included in Schedule III, IV, V or VI shall not be dispensed without an electronic prescription from a practitioner. Under s. 23(g) prescribers shall issue an electronic prescription for all controlled substances and medical devices, and the department shall promulgate regulations setting forth standards for electronic prescriptions. Under s. 23(h) THE COMMISSIONER, THROUGH REGULATION, SHALL ESTABLISH EXCEPTIONS to section 17 and subsection (g) authorizing the limited use of a written and oral prescription where appropriate, and the exceptions SHALL BE LIMITED TO: (i) prescriptions issued by veterinarians; (ii) prescriptions issued or dispensed in circumstances where electronic prescribing is not available due to temporary technological or electrical failure; (iii) a time-limited waiver process for practitioners who demonstrate economic hardship, technological limitations that are not reasonably within the control of the practitioner, or other exceptional circumstance; (iv) prescriptions that are issued or dispensed in emergency situations as defined by the commissioner pursuant to said section 17, including situations where the electronic prescription requirement would result in a delay that would adversely impact the patient's medical condition; (v) when a prescription cannot be issued electronically under federal or state law or regulations; (vi) prescriptions issued outside the jurisdiction of the commonwealth; and (vii) other exceptions to said section 17 and said subsection (g) as the commissioner determines necessary, provided that 90 days before promulgating or amending any regulations regarding other exceptions the commissioner files a written report setting forth the justification with the house and senate committees on ways and means, the joint committee on public health, and the joint committee on mental health, substance use and recovery.
exceptions: Section 17(b) permits written or oral dispensing of a schedule II through VI substance in emergency situations as defined by the commissioner, in accordance with section 20 and related regulations.
The s. 23(h) exceptions take effect as the commissioner establishes them through regulation rather than directly from the statute.

authority.name: DCP Electronic Prescribing and Dispensing Manual, dispensing schedule VI ePrescriptions and Failovers
authority.section: DCP 19-12-108; Dispensing Schedule VI ePrescriptions - Failovers

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: DPH Circular DCP 19-12-108, the Electronic Prescribing and Dispensing Manual, states that a Failover results when a prescriber issues an electronic prescription for a schedule VI controlled substance and that electronic prescription is converted and transmitted to a pharmacy as a computer-generated facsimile due to a defect in the electronic prescribing system beyond the prescriber's control or awareness, and that the resulting computer-generated facsimile DOES NOT QUALIFY AS AN ELECTRONIC PRESCRIPTION and frequently does not meet the signature requirements of a written prescription because the electronic signature appears encoded. It states that the ePrescribing regulation allows a pharmacist to dispense a Failover as a valid oral prescription if the listed process is followed, the last condition being that THE FAILOVER MUST NOT BE FOR AN ADDITIONAL DRUG, giving gabapentin as the example. IN THE EVENT THAT A PHARMACIST RECEIVES A FAILOVER PRESCRIPTION FOR GABAPENTIN, OR ANY OTHER MEDICATION DESIGNATED AS AN ADDITIONAL DRUG, THE PHARMACIST MAY NOT DISPENSE THE MEDICATION, AND INSTEAD MUST CONTACT THE PRESCRIBER FOR A NEW WRITTEN OR ORAL PRESCRIPTION. NO ADDITIONAL WRITTEN FOLLOW-UP IS REQUIRED FOR A FAILOVER DISPENSED AS AN ORAL PRESCRIPTION.
exceptions: A Failover dispensed as a valid oral prescription requires no additional written follow-up.

full_prose_under_review.title: Controlled Substance Schedule Overview
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: Federal schedules and Massachusetts Schedule VI
learning_objectives: Separate federal controlled-substance status from Massachusetts scheduling consequences.
Identify the legal consequence that actually controls instead of reasoning from a schedule label alone.

orientation.text: Controlled-substance classification is a lookup rather than a judgement about how a drug behaves. Federal law collects the schedules established by section 202 of the Controlled Substances Act into 21 CFR Part 1308, one section per schedule: 1308.11 for Schedule I, 1308.12 for Schedule II, 1308.13 for Schedule III, 1308.14 for Schedule IV and 1308.15 for Schedule V. Each of those sections opens with the same sentence -- the schedule 'shall consist of the drugs and other substances, by whatever official name, common or usual name, chemical name, or brand name designated, listed in this section' -- and most of them go on to state that each drug or substance has been assigned the Controlled Substances Code Number set forth opposite it. Membership therefore turns on what the words of a listing reach. Some listings name a substance; others describe a class, as 21 CFR 1308.12(b)(1) reaches 'opium and opiate, and any salt, compound, derivative, or preparation of opium or opiate' before naming the substances it excludes. A class term carries the definition the law gives it rather than its clinical sense: under 21 CFR 1300.01(a) a term Part 1300 does not define takes the meaning set out in 21 U.S.C. 802, and 21 U.S.C. 802(18) defines 'opiate' by an addiction-forming or addiction-sustaining liability similar to morphine. That is why a drug-specific question has to be answered from the exact schedule provision, read with its defined terms and its own exclusions, rather than from a drug's pharmacologic family or an undifferentiated reference to Part 1308.

In Massachusetts the lookup runs through those same federal lists. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 2(a) directs the Commissioner to establish by regulation five schedules incorporating the five federal schedules, and a sixth schedule which shall include all prescription drugs not included in the first five. 105 CMR 700.002 carries that out: 700.002(A) provides that Massachusetts Schedule I consists of the drugs and other substances, by whatever official name, common or usual name, chemical name, or brand name designated, listed in 21 CFR 1308.11, and (B) through (E) repeat that formula for 1308.12 through 1308.15 in turn. As the regulation is currently written, then, Massachusetts Schedules I through V hold exactly what the federal sections list, and a drug's federal listing settles its Massachusetts schedule without a second scheduling decision to look up. The statute still leaves Massachusetts free to act on its own: under s. 2(a1/2) the Commissioner may delete or reschedule substances by regulation, and must issue a regulation controlling a newly federally controlled substance in a corresponding schedule not more than 30 days after the federal notice or statute; and under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 2A the Commissioner may, on the findings that section requires and by an order taking effect after a 14-day notice period, place a substance in Schedule I on a temporary basis, for up to one year. So the lookup is always to the Massachusetts schedules in force, and it is 105 CMR 700.002 in its present form that makes Schedules I through V the federal lists.

105 CMR 700.002(F) provides that Schedule VI consists of all prescription drugs which are not included in any other schedule established by the Commissioner. It is a residual category defined by exclusion, so nothing about a drug's own pharmacology puts it there; a prescription drug reaches Schedule VI precisely because the federal lists that Massachusetts Schedules I through V incorporate do not reach it. What follows next is the point candidates most often get backwards. Schedule VI is a schedule of controlled substances: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 defines a controlled substance as a drug, substance, controlled substance analogue or immediate precursor in any schedule or class referred to in that chapter, and s. 2(a) makes the sixth schedule one of those schedules, so every Schedule VI drug is a controlled substance under Massachusetts law. What it lacks is federal status: because Massachusetts Schedules I through V currently adopt 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15 whole, a drug that reaches Schedule VI is one no federal schedule lists, and Schedule VI status does not by itself make a drug federally controlled. The accurate picture is a Massachusetts controlled-substance schedule with no federal counterpart, not a set of drugs sitting outside controlled-substance law. A Massachusetts rule written for controlled substances reaches Schedule VI unless the rule carves Schedule VI out -- M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(f), for instance, forbids refilling any controlled-substance prescription unless the original provides for refilling and specifies the number of refills -- while a rule written for Schedules II through V does not reach Schedule VI by those words.

Monitoring is the consequence most often attached to the wrong label, in both directions. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(a)(1) directs the Department to maintain an electronic system monitoring the prescribing and dispensing of all schedule II to V, inclusive, controlled substances and certain additional drugs, and defines additional drugs as substances the Department determines to carry a bona fide potential for abuse; 105 CMR 700.001 defines an Additional Drug as a controlled substance in Schedule VI so determined. The reporting regulation follows the same line: 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) applies to every pharmacy registered with the Commissioner that dispenses, pursuant to a prescription, a controlled substance in Schedules II through V or one the Department has classified as an additional drug, and to an out-of-state pharmacy delivering such a substance to a person in Massachusetts, while 700.012(A)(2) takes dispensing pursuant to a medication order to a hospital inpatient outside the regulation altogether. A Schedule VI drug becomes reportable when the Commissioner determines under 105 CMR 700.012(C)(8) that it is an additional drug, weighing factors such as a risk of addiction, known recreational use, known regular diversion for misuse or a known contribution to overdose, and notifies all dispensers that they must begin to report it. Two conclusions follow: a drug can be reportable without appearing in any federal schedule, and a Schedule VI drug is not reportable merely because it is in Schedule VI.

Two disciplines follow from that architecture. The first is to finish the classification properly: the schedule paragraphs in 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15 are typically prefaced 'Unless specifically excepted or unless listed in another schedule', and a number of the listings turn on quantity and formulation rather than on the active ingredient alone, so the thing being classified is the product in hand and not the molecule's reputation. The second is to treat the schedule as a premise. It identifies which body of dispensing, refill, transfer, partial-fill, record and reporting rules must now be opened, and those rules supply the answers. A rule may attach its consequence to a schedule directly, but it is the rule that states the consequence, and the same label can carry different consequences in the two sovereigns. A candidate who stops at the label has done the lookup and skipped the rule.
